Title: Influence of isolation measures for patients with mild symptoms on the spread of COVID-19.
Authors: Pan Q, Gao T, He M.
Citation: Chaos Solitons Fractals. 2020 Oct;139:110022. doi: 10.1016/j.chaos.2020.110022. Epub 2020 Jun 30.
Abstract: During the transmission of COVID-19, the hospital isolation of patients with mild symptoms has been a concern. In this paper, we use a differential equation model to describe the propagation of COVID-19, and discuss the effects of intensity of hospital isolation and moment of taking measures on development of the epidemic. The results show that isolation measures can significantly reduce the epidemic final size and the number of dead, and the greater the intensity of measures, the better, but duration of the epidemic will be prolonged. Whenever isolation measures are taken, the epidemic final size and the number of dead can be reduced. In early stage of the epidemic, taking measures one day later has little impact, but after a certain period, if taking measures one day later, the epidemic final size and the number of dead increase sharply. Taking measures as early as possible makes the maximum number of patients appear later, which is conducive to expanding medical bed resources and reducing the pressure on medical resource demand. As long as possible, high-intensity isolation measures should be taken in time for patients with mild symptoms.
Keywords: Covid-19; Differential equation model; Isolation measure; Patients with mild symptoms; The reproduction number
overall_justification: The study is clearly about COVID-19 and explicitly references the reproduction number in the keywords, suggesting transmission quantification is part of the work. However, based on the abstract it primarily evaluates isolation measures via a differential equation model and does not clearly indicate estimation of R0 from empirical outbreak data, making its evidentiary contribution to an R0 review uncertain/likely limited.
disease_justification: Title/abstract explicitly focus on COVID-19 transmission and control measures during the COVID-19 epidemic.
population_justification: Focuses on patients with mild symptoms and epidemic spread in humans (hospital isolation policies).
location_justification: No specific geographic setting is stated in the title/abstract; could be a general modeling study.
evidence_justification: Appears to be a compartmental/differential-equation modeling analysis; the abstract does not state calibration to real-world data or reporting new empirical estimates.
transmission_justification: Keywords explicitly include 'The reproduction number', but the abstract does not clearly report an R0 estimate or specific reproduction-number results.

Title: Compounding crises of social reproduction: Microfinance, over-indebtedness and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Authors: Brickell K, Picchioni F, Natarajan N, Guermond V, Parsons L, Zanello G, Bateman M.
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has hit at a time when microfinance is at its historical peak, with an estimated 139 million microfinance customers globally. Cambodia's microfinance sector is one of the fastest growing, and like others in the Global South has moved from offering entrepreneurial capital to everyday liquidity, and even disaster relief. In this Viewpoint, however, we argue that the promotion of microfinance as market-based relief and recovery from the pandemic should be a source of concern, not comfort. We firstly suggest that as a result of the health and economic impacts associated with COVID-19, credit-taking is likely to escalate further in terms of the number of borrowers and loan amounts. Second, we contend that a growing reliance on MFIs will leave households undernourished, and further vulnerable to its disciplining and extractive impulses. Third, we argue that the interplay between over-indebtedness, pre-existing malnutrition challenges, and the global public health crisis of COVID-19 represents a major challenge to gender equality and sustainable development. Coordination between the Cambodian government, microfinance lenders, international investors, and development partners is vital to offer debt relief. Furthermore, to reverse the reliance of so many households on the microfinance industry for survival, inclusive socio-economic policies and public welfare services must be prioritised.
Keywords: Asia; COVID19; Cambodia; Microfinance; Over-indebtedness; Social reproduction
overall_justification: Although COVID-19 is central, the paper focuses on social/economic impacts (microfinance, over-indebtedness) rather than SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics. It does not mention or estimate R0/reproduction numbers and appears to be non-empirical commentary, making it unlikely to inform the review question.
disease_justification: COVID-19 is explicitly discussed throughout as the context for health and economic impacts.
population_justification: Discusses households/borrowers and social impacts in Cambodia (human populations), though not in an epidemiologic transmission context.
location_justification: Clearly situated in Cambodia (and broader Global South context).
evidence_justification: This is explicitly a “Viewpoint” piece arguing policy concerns about microfinance during COVID-19; it does not report new empirical data or estimate epidemiologic parameters.
transmission_justification: No mention of reproductive number/reproduction number/R0 or any transmission quantification; “social reproduction” is a different concept than epidemiologic reproduction number.

Title: Is it safe to lift COVID-19 travel bans? The Newfoundland story.
Authors: Linka K, Rahman P, Goriely A, Kuhl E.
Abstract: A key strategy to prevent a local outbreak during the COVID-19 pandemic is to restrict incoming travel. Once a region has successfully contained the disease, it becomes critical to decide when and how to reopen the borders. Here we explore the impact of border reopening for the example of Newfoundland and Labrador, a Canadian province that has enjoyed no new cases since late April, 2020. We combine a network epidemiology model with machine learning to infer parameters and predict the COVID-19 dynamics upon partial and total airport reopening, with perfect and imperfect quarantine conditions. Our study suggests that upon full reopening, every other day, a new COVID-19 case would enter the province. Under the current conditions, banning air travel from outside Canada is more efficient in managing the pandemic than fully reopening and quarantining 95% of the incoming population. Our study provides quantitative insights of the efficacy of travel restrictions and can inform political decision making in the controversy of reopening.
Keywords: COVID-19; Epidemiology; Machine learning; Reproduction number; SEIR model
overall_justification: The paper explicitly models COVID-19 transmission dynamics in Newfoundland and Labrador and uses an SEIR/network model framework. Although the keywords include “Reproduction number,” the abstract does not explicitly report/estimate R0 (or Rt) values, focusing instead on border reopening scenarios and imported case counts, making transmission-metric relevance uncertain. It appears to be an original, data-calibrated modeling study (parameters inferred via machine learning), but details of empirical data sources are not explicit in the abstract.
disease_justification: Explicitly about COVID-19, border reopening, and COVID-19 dynamics in Newfoundland and Labrador.
population_justification: Focuses on travel-related introductions and COVID-19 dynamics in a human population (province-level policy context).
location_justification: Clearly set in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada.
evidence_justification: Uses modeling with parameter inference via machine learning to predict dynamics under reopening/quarantine scenarios, suggesting an original empirical-calibrated analysis, though specific data inputs are not described in the abstract.
transmission_justification: Keyword lists “Reproduction number,” but the abstract does not explicitly state R0/Rt estimates or numeric reproduction numbers; emphasis is on travel bans and predicted imported cases.

Title: Probabilistic approximation of effective reproduction number of COVID-19 using daily death statistics.
Authors: Na J, Tibebu H, De Silva V, Kondoz A, Caine M.
Citation: Chaos Solitons Fractals. 2020 Nov;140:110181. doi: 10.1016/j.chaos.2020.110181. Epub 2020 Jul 30.
Abstract: The effective reproduction number (R) which signifies the number of secondary cases infected by one infectious individual, is an important measure of the spread of an infectious disease. Due to the dynamics of COVID-19 where many infected people are not showing symptoms or showing mild symptoms, and where different countries are employing different testing strategies, it is quite difficult to calculate the R, while the pandemic is still widespread. This paper presents a probabilistic methodology to evaluate the effective reproduction number by considering only the daily death statistics of a given country. The methodology utilizes a linearly constrained Quadratic Programming scheme to estimate the daily new infection cases from the daily death statistics, based on the probability distribution of delays associated with symptom onset and to reporting a death. The proposed methodology is validated in-silico by simulating an infectious disease through a Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) model. The results suggest that with a reasonable estimate of distribution of delay to death from the onset of symptoms, the model can provide accurate estimates of R. The proposed method is then used to estimate the R values for two countries.
overall_justification: Directly targets estimation of the effective reproduction number for COVID-19 and applies the approach to country-level death data, making it potentially relevant. However, the abstract emphasizes in-silico validation and provides limited detail on real-world data/estimates, so it is unclear how much original empirical evidence is reported and whether it provides R0 (vs time-varying R).
disease_justification: Title and abstract explicitly focus on COVID-19 and estimating its effective reproduction number using COVID-19 daily death statistics.
population_justification: Uses country-level daily death statistics from COVID-19, which implies human population data (not animal/in vitro).
location_justification: Uses daily death statistics for “a given country” and applies the method to estimate R for two countries, but the specific locations are not named in the abstract.
evidence_justification: Appears to be primarily a methodological/modeling paper with in-silico SIR validation; it also applies the method to real countries’ death statistics, but the abstract does not clearly state data sources/timeframes or report specific empirical estimates.
transmission_justification: Explicitly estimates the effective reproduction number (R) for COVID-19 and discusses methodology to calculate R from death statistics.

Title: Modelling the Evolution of COVID-19 in High-Incidence European Countries and Regions: Estimated Number of Infections and Impact of Past and Future Intervention Measures.
Authors: Fernández-Recio J.
Abstract: A previously developed mechanistic model of COVID-19 transmission has been adapted and applied here to study the evolution of the disease and the effect of intervention measures in some European countries and territories where the disease has had a major impact. A clear impact of the major intervention measures on the reproduction number (Rt) has been found in all studied countries and territories, as already suggested by the drop in the number of deaths over time. Interestingly, the impact of such major intervention measures seems to be the same in most of these countries. The model has also provided realistic estimates of the total number of infections, active cases and future outcomes. While the predictive capabilities of the model are much more uncertain before the peak of the outbreak, we could still reliably predict the evolution of the disease after a major intervention by assuming the subsequent reproduction number from the current study. A greater challenge is to foresee the long-term impact of softer intervention measures, but this model can estimate the outcome of different scenarios and help to plan changes for the implementation of control measures in a given country or region.
Keywords: COVID-19; disease transmission model; epidemiology; intervention measures; virus
overall_justification: The study is clearly about COVID-19 and explicitly estimates reproduction numbers (Rt) in multiple European settings, relating changes to intervention measures. However, the research question targets R0 specifically; the abstract emphasizes time-varying Rt and intervention effects, and the level of clearly described original empirical calibration/data in the abstract is limited.
disease_justification: Explicitly investigates COVID-19 transmission and evolution in European countries and regions.
population_justification: Focuses on COVID-19 evolution, infections, deaths, and interventions in countries/territories, implying human population transmission.
location_justification: Conducted in high-incidence European countries and regions/territories (specific locales not listed in the provided text but clearly geographic).
evidence_justification: Uses a mechanistic transmission model adapted and applied to real-country epidemic trajectories (e.g., deaths over time) to estimate infections and Rt; original model-based empirical estimation, but data sources/details are not provided in the abstract.
transmission_justification: Explicitly discusses the reproduction number, specifically Rt, and how interventions impact it across studied settings.

Title: Effectiveness of Interventions to Control Transmission of Reemergent Cases of COVID-19 - Jilin Province, China, 2020.
Authors: Zhao Q, Yang M, Wang Y, Yao L, Qiao J, Cheng Z, Liu H, Liu X, Zhu Y, Zhao Z, Rui J, Chen T.
Abstract: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ABOUT THIS TOPIC?: COVID-19 has a high transmissibility calculated by mathematical model. The dynamics of the disease and the effectiveness of intervention to control the transmission remain unclear in Jilin Province, China. WHAT IS ADDED BY THIS REPORT?: This is the first study to report the dynamic characteristics and to quantify the effectiveness of interventions implemented in the second outbreak of COVID-19 in Jilin Province, China. The effective reproduction number of the disease before and after May 10 was 4.00 and p<0.01, respectively. The combined interventions reduced the transmissibility of COVID-19 by 99% and the number of cases by 98.36%. WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH PRACTICE?: The findings of this study would add data on the transmission of COVID-19 and provide evidence to prepare the second outbreak transmission of the disease in other areas of China even in many other countries.
overall_justification: The paper is clearly about COVID-19 transmission in a defined human population in Jilin, China, and explicitly reports an effective reproduction number before/after interventions. However, it emphasizes the effective reproduction number (Rt) rather than explicitly estimating the basic reproduction number (R0), so it is better treated as a possible candidate for an R0-focused review.
disease_justification: Explicitly investigates COVID-19 transmission and interventions during reemergent cases in Jilin Province.
population_justification: Focuses on COVID-19 cases and transmission in a provincial outbreak, which implies human population surveillance (no animal/in vitro elements mentioned).
location_justification: Study is explicitly set in Jilin Province, China (2020).
evidence_justification: Appears to quantify intervention effectiveness and changes in transmission during a specific outbreak, implying analysis of outbreak data, but the abstract provides limited details on data sources/methods.
transmission_justification: Explicitly reports the effective reproduction number before and after May 10 and discusses transmissibility reduction due to interventions (transmission quantification is central).

Title: Identification and estimation of the SEIRD epidemic model for COVID-19.
Authors: Korolev I.
Abstract: This paper studies the SEIRD epidemic model for COVID-19. First, I show that the model is poorly identified from the observed number of deaths and confirmed cases. There are many sets of parameters that are observationally equivalent in the short run but lead to markedly different long run forecasts. Second, I show that the basic reproduction number R 0 can be identified from the data, conditional on epidemiologic parameters, and propose several nonlinear SUR approaches to estimate R 0 . I examine the performance of these methods using Monte Carlo studies and demonstrate that they yield fairly accurate estimates of R 0 . Next, I apply these methods to estimate R 0 for the US, California, and Japan, and document heterogeneity in the value of R 0 across regions. My estimation approach accounts for possible underreporting of the number of cases. I demonstrate that if one fails to take underreporting into account and estimates R 0 from the reported cases data, the resulting estimate of R 0 may be biased downward and the resulting forecasts may exaggerate the long run number of deaths. Finally, I discuss how auxiliary information from random tests can be used to calibrate the initial parameters of the model and narrow down the range of possible forecasts of the future number of deaths.
Keywords: COVID-19; Parameter identification; SEIR model; Seemingly unrelated equations
overall_justification: The study explicitly aims to identify and estimate the basic reproduction number (R0) for COVID-19 and applies the approach to empirical data from multiple regions (US, California, Japan). It is not a review/commentary; it presents an estimation approach calibrated/fit to observed cases/deaths and discusses underreporting impacts on R0.
disease_justification: Title/abstract explicitly study the SEIRD epidemic model for COVID-19 and discuss estimation using COVID-19 cases and deaths.
population_justification: Uses human epidemiological surveillance data (confirmed cases and deaths) for populations in the US/California/Japan.
location_justification: Applies estimation to specific geographic settings: the US, California, and Japan.
evidence_justification: Reports original estimation methods and applies them to real-world reported cases/deaths data (plus Monte Carlo performance evaluation).
transmission_justification: Explicitly focuses on identifying and estimating the basic reproduction number R0, including proposing methods and presenting estimated R0 values across regions.

Title: A novel deterministic forecast model for COVID-19 epidemic based on a single ordinary integro-differential equation.
Authors: Köhler-Rieper F, Röhl CHF, De Micheli E.
Abstract: In this paper, we present a new approach to deterministic modelling of COVID-19 epidemic. Our model dynamics is expressed by a single prognostic variable which satisfies an integro-differential equation. All unknown parameters are described with a single, time-dependent variable R(t). We show that our model has similarities to classic compartmental models, such as SIR, and that the variable R(t) can be interpreted as a generalized effective reproduction number. The advantages of our approach are the simplicity of having only one equation, the numerical stability due to an integral formulation and the reliability since the model is formulated in terms of the most trustable statistical data variable: the number of cumulative diagnosed positive cases of COVID-19. Once this dynamic variable is calculated, other non-dynamic variables, such as the number of heavy cases (hospital beds), the number of intensive-care cases (ICUs) and the fatalities, can be derived from it using a similarly stable, integral approach. The formulation with a single equation allows us to calculate from real data the values of the sample effective reproduction number, which can then be fitted. Extrapolated values of R(t) can be used in the model to make reliable forecasts, though under the assumption that measures for reducing infections are maintained. We have applied our model to more than 15 countries and the ongoing results are available on a web-based platform [1]. In this paper, we focus on the data for two exemplary countries, Italy and Germany, and show that the model is capable of reproducing the course of the epidemic in the past and forecasting its course for a period of four to five weeks with a reasonable numerical stability.
overall_justification: COVID-19 is the central focus and the study estimates a reproduction-number-type metric (effective R(t)) from empirical case data in Italy/Germany (and other countries). It does not clearly aim to estimate the basic reproduction number R0 specifically, but may still provide transmissibility estimates relevant to the review depending on whether effective R is eligible.
disease_justification: The paper explicitly models the COVID-19 epidemic and references diagnosed positive COVID-19 cases.
population_justification: Uses national COVID-19 surveillance data (cumulative diagnosed cases, hospitalizations/ICU/fatalities), which are human population outcomes.
location_justification: Applies the model to multiple countries and specifically analyzes Italy and Germany.
evidence_justification: Reports an original modeling approach calibrated with real-world case data across countries and calculates sample effective reproduction numbers from these data.
transmission_justification: Explicitly defines and estimates a time-dependent R(t) interpreted as a generalized effective reproduction number from real data; however the focus is on effective R(t) rather than explicitly reporting the basic reproduction number R0.

Title: A novel covid-19 mathematical model with fractional derivatives: Singular and nonsingular kernels.
Authors: Zhang Z.
Citation: Chaos Solitons Fractals. 2020 Oct;139:110060. doi: 10.1016/j.chaos.2020.110060. Epub 2020 Jun 28.
Abstract: In this paper, we considered a new mathematical model depicting the possibility of spread within a given general population. The model is constructed with five classes including susceptible, exposed, infected, recovered and deaths. We presented a detailed analysis of the suggested model including, the derivation of equilibrium points endemic and disease-free, reproductive number using the next generation matrix, the stability analysis of the equilibrium points and finally the positiveness of the model solutions. The model was extended to the concept of fractional differentiation to capture different memories including power law, decay and crossover behaviors. A numerical method based on the Newton was used to provide numerical solutions for different memories.
Keywords: Fractional calculus; Local and global asymptotic stability; New mathematical model for covid-19; Stability analysis and reproductive number
overall_justification: The paper is explicitly about COVID-19 and includes derivation of a “reproductive number” (next-generation matrix) in an SEIRD-style compartmental model. However, from the abstract it appears primarily methodological/theoretical (fractional-derivative model and stability analysis) without clear indication of calibration to real-world COVID-19 data, making the presence of original empirical estimation of R0 uncertain.
disease_justification: Title, keywords, and abstract explicitly focus on COVID-19 and propose a COVID-19 transmission model.
population_justification: Refers to a “general population” SEIRD-type model, implying humans, though no specific human data or subgroup is described.
location_justification: No geographic setting is specified; the model is described generically (location not stated).
evidence_justification: Presents an original mathematical model and numerical solutions, but the abstract does not indicate fitting/calibration to empirical COVID-19 data or reporting data-derived R0 estimates.
transmission_justification: Explicitly derives the reproductive number using the next-generation matrix and discusses stability around disease-free/endemic equilibria.

Title: What Can We Estimate From Fatality and Infectious Case Data Using the Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) Model? A Case Study of Covid-19 Pandemic.
Authors: Ahmetolan S, Bilge AH, Demirci A, Peker-Dobie A, Ergonul O.
Abstract: The rapidly spreading Covid-19 that affected almost all countries, was first reported at the end of 2019. As a consequence of its highly infectious nature, countries all over the world have imposed extremely strict measures to control its spread. Since the earliest stages of this major pandemic, academics have done a huge amount of research in order to understand the disease, develop medication, vaccines and tests, and model its spread. Among these studies, a great deal of effort has been invested in the estimation of epidemic parameters in the early stage, for the countries affected by Covid-19, hence to predict the course of the epidemic but the variability of the controls over the course of the epidemic complicated the modeling processes. In this article, the determination of the basic reproduction number, the mean duration of the infectious period, the estimation of the timing of the peak of the epidemic wave is discussed using early phase data. Daily case reports and daily fatalities for China, South Korea, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Iran, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States over the period January 22, 2020-April 18, 2020 are evaluated using the Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) model. For each country, the SIR models fitting cumulative infective case data within 5% error are analyzed. It is observed that the basic reproduction number and the mean duration of the infectious period can be estimated only in cases where the spread of the epidemic is over (for China and South Korea in the present case). Nevertheless, it is shown that the timing of the maximum and timings of the inflection points of the proportion of infected individuals can be robustly estimated from the normalized data. The validation of the estimates by comparing the predictions with actual data has shown that the predictions were realized for all countries except USA, as long as lock-down measures were retained.
Keywords: COVID-19; SIR model; epidemiology; mathematical models; parameter estimation
overall_justification: The study explicitly focuses on COVID-19 and discusses estimating the basic reproduction number using country-level case and fatality time series calibrated with an SIR model. It uses original empirical data across multiple human populations and locations, and R0 estimation is a stated objective (at least for countries where the wave ended).
disease_justification: Explicitly about the COVID-19 pandemic (“Covid-19”, “pandemic”), using case and fatality data from multiple countries.
population_justification: Analyzes national-level reported COVID-19 cases/fatalities, implying human populations (general population).
location_justification: Includes multiple real-world geographic settings (e.g., China, South Korea, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Iran, Turkey, UK, USA).
evidence_justification: Uses empirical daily case reports and fatalities (Jan 22–Apr 18, 2020) from multiple countries and fits SIR models to observed data; reports parameter estimates.
transmission_justification: Explicitly discusses and aims to determine the basic reproduction number (R0) using early phase data and SIR model fitting.

Title: Insights into the dynamics and control of COVID-19 infection rates.
Authors: Willis MJ, Díaz VHG, Prado-Rubio OA, von Stosch M.
Citation: Chaos Solitons Fractals. 2020 Sep;138:109937. doi: 10.1016/j.chaos.2020.109937. Epub 2020 May 28.
Abstract: This work aims to model, simulate and provide insights into the dynamics and control of COVID-19 infection rates. Using an established epidemiological model augmented with a time-varying disease transmission rate allows daily model calibration using COVID-19 case data from countries around the world. This hybrid model provides predictive forecasts of the cumulative number of infected cases. It also reveals the dynamics associated with disease suppression, demonstrating the time to reduce the effective, time-dependent, reproduction number. Model simulations provide insights into the outcomes of disease suppression measures and the predicted duration of the pandemic. Visualisation of reported data provides up-to-date condition monitoring, while daily model calibration allows for a continued and updated forecast of the current state of the pandemic.
Keywords: COVID-19; Model calibration; Predictive modelling and simulation; Time varying disease transmission rate
overall_justification: Disease (COVID-19) and reproduction-number content are explicit and central, including discussion of a time-dependent reproduction number. However, based on the abstract it is unclear whether the paper reports original estimated R0/Rt values as results (versus describing a calibrated forecasting approach), so it fits better as a possible rather than strong candidate.
disease_justification: The study focus is explicitly COVID-19 throughout the title, keywords, and abstract.
population_justification: Uses COVID-19 case data from multiple countries, implying human populations (confirmed cases). No indication of animal/in vitro work.
location_justification: Mentions using case data from "countries around the world" (multi-country, real-world setting), though specific countries are not named in the abstract.
evidence_justification: Appears to calibrate an epidemiological model using reported case data, but the abstract does not clearly state new estimated R0/Rt values or primary empirical estimation results versus a general modeling/forecasting framework.
transmission_justification: Explicitly mentions the effective, time-dependent reproduction number and modeling disease transmission dynamics in relation to suppression measures.

Title: Estimation of basic reproduction number for COVID-19 and the reasons for its differences.
Authors: Najafimehr H, Mohamed Ali K, Safari S, Yousefifard M, Hosseini M.
Citation: Int J Clin Pract. 2020 Aug;74(8):e13518. doi: 10.1111/ijcp.13518.
overall_justification: 该文与COVID-19及R0高度相关，并给出多项已发表研究中的R0取值范围与方法差异讨论。然而其为来信性质的综述性总结，未提供新的经验数据或原创R0估计，因此不满足“原创实证证据”的核心要求，整体更适合作为背景参考而非纳入估计研究。

location_justification: 提及中国、意大利及“海外”等地区的R0范围，但本文并非基于某一特定地点的数据开展研究，更多为概述性讨论。
evidence_justification: 文章类型为Letter，主要汇总/讨论既有研究的R0结果与差异原因，未呈现新的原始数据分析或新的R0估计。

Title: Effects of control measures on the dynamics of COVID-19 and double-peak behavior in Spain.
Authors: Huang J, Qi G.
Abstract: The COVID-19 disease significantly has threatened the human lives and economy. It is a dynamic system with transmission and control as factors. Modeling the dynamics of the spread of COVID-19 based on the reported data can predict the growing trend of such a disease. In this paper, the dynamic evolution of COVID-19 in Spain is studied, and a comprehensive SEIR model is adopted to fit the obtained clinical progressive data of COVID-19 in Spain. The transmission rate between the susceptible and the self-quarantine susceptible is made to be time-variant, which is reasonable. The equilibria are found, and the stability condition is given using the basic reproduction number and eigenvalues at the points. The effect on daily confirmed cases for the transmission rate from susceptible to the exposed population due to the currently exposed and infectious is extensively investigated. The risk of the easing of the control measure is investigated. The double-peak dynamic behavior of the COVID-19 system is observed. The second wave rebound shows that the daily confirmed cases of the second peak even much higher than the first peak.
Keywords: COVID-19; Disease transmission rate; Double-peak dynamics; Modeling
overall_justification: The paper is explicitly about COVID-19 transmission dynamics in humans in Spain and uses an SEIR model fitted to reported data. It mentions the basic reproduction number in the context of equilibria/stability, but the abstract does not clearly indicate that estimating R0 (with values) is a primary reported result; R0 may be used mainly as a theoretical threshold parameter.
disease_justification: COVID-19 is the explicit focus throughout the title/abstract/keywords.
population_justification: Focuses on population-level COVID-19 spread and daily confirmed cases, which are human surveillance data.
location_justification: Study explicitly analyzes COVID-19 dynamics in Spain.
evidence_justification: Uses a SEIR model fitted to reported/clinical progression data (daily confirmed cases) in Spain, implying original estimation calibrated to real-world data rather than a narrative review.
transmission_justification: Explicitly references the basic reproduction number as part of the model’s equilibria and stability analysis, but the abstract does not state an estimated R0 value or emphasize R0 estimation as the main objective.

Title: Meteorological conditions and nonpharmaceutical interventions jointly determined local transmissibility of COVID-19 in 41 Chinese cities: A retrospective observational study.
Authors: Fang LQ, Zhang HY, Zhao H, Che TL, Zhang AR, Liu MJ, Shi WQ, Guo JP, Zhang Y, Liu W, Yang Y.
Citation: Lancet Reg Health West Pac. 2020 Sep;2:100020. doi: 10.1016/j.lanwpc.2020.100020. Epub 2020 Sep 6.
Journal/Book: The Lancet regional health. Western Pacific
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Before effective vaccines become widely available, sufficient understanding of the impacts of climate, human movement and non-pharmaceutical interventions on the transmissibility of COVID-19 is needed but still lacking. METHODS: We collected by crowdsourcing a database of 11 003 COVID-19 cases from 305 cities outside Hubei Province from December 31, 2019 to April 27, 2020. We estimated the daily effective reproduction numbers (Rt ) of COVID-19 in 41 cities where the crowdsourced case data are comparable to the official surveillance data. The impacts of meteorological variables, human movement indices and nonpharmaceutical emergency responses on Rt were evaluated with generalized estimation equation models. FINDINGS: The median Rt was 0•46 (IQR: 0•37-0•87) in the northern cities, higher than 0•20 (IQR: 0•09-0•52) in the southern cities (p=0•004). A higher local transmissibility of COVID-19 was associated with a low temperature, a relative humidity near 70-75%, and higher intracity and intercity human movement. An increase in temperature from 0℃ to 20℃ would reduce Rt by 30% (95 CI 10-46%). A further increase to 30℃ would result in another 17% (95% CI 5-27%) reduction. An increase in relative humidity from 40% to 75% would raise the transmissibility by 47% (95% CI 9-97%), but a further increase to 90% would reduce the transmissibility by 12% (95% CI 4-19%). The decrease in intracity human movement as a part of the highest-level emergency response in China reduced the transmissibility by 36% (95% CI 27-44%), compared to 5% (95% CI 1-9%) for restricting intercity transport. Other nonpharmaceutical interventions further reduced Rt by 39% (95% CI 31-47%). INTERPRETATION: Climate can affect the transmission of COVID-19 where effective interventions are implemented. Restrictions on intracity human movement may be needed in places where other nonpharmaceutical interventions are unable to mitigate local transmission. FUNDING: China Mega-Project on Infectious Disease Prevention; U.S. National Institutes of Health and National Science Foundation.
overall_justification: 该研究明确聚焦COVID-19在中国41个城市的“可传播性/传播强度”，并在方法与结果中多次明确估计并分析了每日有效再生数Rt（含具体数值与置信区间），属于与再生数相关的核心研究内容。研究基于真实人群病例数据（众包病例数据库并与官方监测数据可比）进行回顾性观察分析，因此具备较强的原始实证证据。需要注意其指标为Rt（有效再生数）而非R0（基本再生数），但仍与“再生数”问题高度相关。
disease_justification: 全文明确研究对象为COVID-19，数据来源为COVID-19病例，且研究目的为解释其传播性变化。
population_justification: 使用来自305个城市（其中41城用于Rt估计）的COVID-19病例数据，属于人群层面的传播研究。
location_justification: 研究地点明确为中国41个城市（病例来自Hubei以外的305城市数据库），地理信息具体。
evidence_justification: 回顾性观察研究，基于众包病例数据并进行Rt估计与GEE模型分析，提供原始量化结果与置信区间。
transmission_justification: 明确估计“daily effective reproduction numbers (Rt)”并报告中位数、IQR及与气象/干预相关的变化效应；再生数为核心结局。

Title: Global stability and cost-effectiveness analysis of COVID-19 considering the impact of the environment: using data from Ghana.
Authors: Asamoah JKK, Owusu MA, Jin Z, Oduro FT, Abidemi A, Gyasi EO.
Citation: Chaos Solitons Fractals. 2020 Nov;140:110103. doi: 10.1016/j.chaos.2020.110103. Epub 2020 Jul 10.
Abstract: COVID-19 potentially threatens the lives and livelihood of people all over the world. The disease is presently a major health concern in Ghana and the rest of the world. Although, human to human transmission dynamics has been established, not much research is done on the dynamics of the virus in the environment and the role human play by releasing the virus into the environment. Therefore, investigating the human-environment-human by use of mathematical analysis and optimal control theory is relatively necessary. The dynamics of COVID-19 for this study is segregated into compartments as: Susceptible (S), Exposed (E), Asymptomatic (A), Symptomatic (I), Recovered (R) and the Virus in the environment/surfaces (V). The basic reproduction number R 0 without controls is computed. The application of Lyapunov's function is used to analyse the global stability of the proposed model. We fit the model to real data from Ghana in the time window 12th March 2020 to 7th May 2020, with the aid of python programming language using the least-squares method. The average basic reproduction number without controls, R 0 a , is approximately 2.68. An optimal control is formulated based on the sensitivity analysis. Numerical simulation of the model is also done to verify the analytic results. The admissible control set such as: effective testing and quarantine when boarders are opened, the usage of masks and face shields through media education, cleaning of surfaces with home-based detergents, practising proper cough etiquette and fumigating commercial areas; health centers is simulated in MATLAB. We used forward-backward sweep Runge-Kutta scheme which gave interesting results in the main text, for example, the cost-effectiveness analysis shows that, Strategy 4 (safety measures adopted by the asymptomatic and symptomatic individuals such as practicing proper coughing etiquette by maintaining a distance, covering coughs and sneezes with disposable tissues or clothing and washing of hands after coughing or sneezing) is the most cost-effective strategy among all the six control intervention strategies under consideration.
Keywords: COVID-19; Cost-effectiveness analysis; Environmental transmission; Global stability; Optimal control; Sensitivity analysis
overall_justification: The study explicitly estimates COVID-19 R0 and provides a numerical value (≈2.68) derived from a model calibrated to real data from Ghana. It is human-population focused and location-specific, with original empirical model fitting rather than a purely theoretical discussion.
disease_justification: Focuses explicitly on COVID-19 throughout (title/abstract/keywords).
population_justification: Models COVID-19 transmission in humans using human compartments (S, E, A, I, R) and discusses human interventions (testing, masks, hygiene).
location_justification: Uses real-world data from Ghana (12 March 2020 to 7 May 2020) and frames the analysis in the Ghana context.
evidence_justification: Fits a transmission model to empirical Ghana case data using least-squares and reports estimated R0; not a review/commentary.
transmission_justification: Explicitly computes and reports the basic reproduction number R0 (average R0 ≈ 2.68) and states R0 without controls is computed.

Title: Global stability of COVID-19 model involving the quarantine strategy and media coverage effects.
Authors: A Mohsen A, Al-Husseiny HF, Zhou X, Hattaf K.
Citation: AIMS Public Health. 2020 Aug 3;7(3):587-605. doi: 10.3934/publichealth.2020047. eCollection 2020.
Abstract: In this paper, we build and analyze a mathematical model of COVID-19 transmission considering media coverage effects. Due to transmission characteristics of COVID-19, we can divided the population into five classes. The first class describes the susceptible individuals, the second class is exposed individuals, the third class is infected individuals, the fourth class is quarantine class and the last class is recovered individuals. The existence, uniqueness and boundedness of the solutions of the model are discussed. The basic reproduction number ℛ 0 is obtained. All possible equilibrium points of the model are investigated and their local stability is discussed under some conditions. The disease-free equilibrium is local asymptotically stable when ℛ 0 < 1 and unstable when ℛ 0 > 1 . The globally asymptotical stability of all point is verified by Lyapunov function. Finally, numerical simulations are carried out to confirm the analytical results and understand the effect of varying the parameters on spread of COVID-19. These findings suggested that media coverage can be considered as an effective way to mitigate the COVID-19 spreading.
Keywords: COVID-19; backward bifurcation; mathematical modeling; media coverage effect; quarantine
overall_justification: The paper is clearly about COVID-19 and explicitly derives the basic reproduction number ℛ0 as a central objective. However, it appears mainly theoretical and the abstract does not indicate ℛ0 is estimated from empirical outbreak data (more derived from model structure/assumptions), making it less directly informative for an R0 evidence synthesis.
disease_justification: Focuses explicitly on COVID-19 transmission dynamics throughout the model and analysis.
population_justification: Model compartments (susceptible/exposed/infected/quarantined/recovered) represent a human population epidemic framework, though no specific human dataset is described.
location_justification: No geographic setting is specified; appears to be a general (non-location-specific) transmission model.
evidence_justification: Primarily a mathematical modeling/stability analysis paper; mentions numerical simulations but the abstract does not indicate calibration/estimation using real-world empirical data.
transmission_justification: Explicitly derives and analyzes the basic reproduction number (ℛ0) for COVID-19, including stability conditions for ℛ0 < 1 vs > 1.

Title: An age and space structured SIR model describing the Covid-19 pandemic.
Authors: Colombo RM, Garavello M, Marcellini F, Rossi E.
Abstract: UNLABELLED: We present an epidemic model capable of describing key features of the Covid-19 pandemic. While capturing several qualitative properties of the virus spreading, it allows to compute the basic reproduction number, the number of deaths due to the virus and various other statistics. Numerical integrations are used to illustrate the adherence of the evolutions described by the model to specific well known real features of the present pandemic. In particular, this model is consistent with the well known relevance of quarantine, shows the dramatic role of care houses and accounts for the increase in the death toll when spatial movements are not constrained. ELECTRONIC SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL: The online version of this article (10.1186/s13362-020-00090-4) contains supplementary material.
Keywords: Age and Space Structured SIR Model; Covid-19 Modeling; Differential Equations in Epidemic Modeling
overall_justification: COVID-19 is the central topic and the model explicitly allows computation of the basic reproduction number. However, it is unclear whether the paper provides an empirical R0 estimate grounded in observed data versus a theoretical/model-derived quantity, and no specific location is described in the abstract.
disease_justification: Title and abstract explicitly focus on the Covid-19 pandemic and virus spreading.
population_justification: The model is intended to describe the pandemic in populations (age- and space-structured), but the abstract does not explicitly state human data or a defined human cohort.
location_justification: The abstract discusses general pandemic features (e.g., quarantine, care houses, spatial movements) but does not specify any geographic study setting or country/region.
evidence_justification: Appears to be a mathematical SIR modeling paper with numerical integrations; the abstract does not clearly indicate calibration/estimation using real-world empirical data (could be primarily theoretical).
transmission_justification: Explicitly states it allows computation of the basic reproduction number, which is central to the model’s outputs.

Title: Predicting the number of total COVID-19 cases and deaths in Brazil by the Gompertz model.
Authors: Valle JAM.
Abstract: In this work, we estimate the total number of infected and deaths by COVID-19 in Brazil and two Brazilian States (Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo). To obtain the unknown data, we use an iterative method in the Gompertz model, whose formulation is well known in the field of biology. Based on data collected from the Ministry of Health from February 26, 2020, to July 2, 2020, we predict, from July 3 to 9 and at the end of the epidemic, the number of infected and killed for the whole country and for the Brazilian states of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. We estimate, until July 9, 2020, a total of 1,709,755 cases and 65,384 deaths in Brazil, 331,718 cases and 15,621 deaths in Sao Paulo, 134,454 cases and 11,574 deaths in Rio de Janeiro. We also estimate the basic reproduction number R 0 for Brazil and its two states. The estimated values ( R 0 ) were 1.3, 1.3, and 1.4 for Brazil, Sao Paulo, and Rio de Janeiro, respectively. The results show a good fit between the observed data and those obtained by the Gompertz. The proposed methodology can also be applied to other countries and Brazilian states, and we provide an executable as well as the source code for a straightforward application of the method on such data.
Keywords: Covid-19; Inverse problem; Minimal error method; Model Gompertz
overall_justification: Directly focused on COVID-19 in humans in Brazil and explicitly reports estimated R0 values. The analysis uses real-world case/death data and a fitted model, meeting the core relevance dimensions for estimating COVID-19 reproduction number.
disease_justification: The study explicitly analyzes COVID-19 cases and deaths and models the epidemic trajectory in Brazil and specific states.
population_justification: Uses human COVID-19 case and death counts from Brazil and two states (Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo), implying a human population focus.
location_justification: Conducted using surveillance data from Brazil, including Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, with clear geographic context.
evidence_justification: Uses empirical Ministry of Health data (Feb 26–Jul 2, 2020) and fits a Gompertz model to estimate totals and R0; appears to be an original modeling analysis calibrated to real-world data.
transmission_justification: Explicitly estimates the basic reproduction number (R0) and reports numerical R0 values for Brazil and two states.

Title: Are women leaders significantly better at controlling the contagion during the COVID-19 pandemic?
Authors: Purkayastha S, Salvatore M, Mukherjee B.
Journal/Book: Journal of health and social sciences
Abstract: Recent media articles have suggested that women-led countries are doing better in terms of their responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. We examine an ensemble of public health metrics to assess the control of COVID-19 epidemic in women-versus men-led countries worldwide based on data available up to June 3. The median of the distribution of median time-varying effective reproduction number for women- and men-led countries were 0.89 and 1.14 respectively with the 95% two-sample bootstrap-based confidence interval for the difference (women - men) being [-0.34, 0.02]. In terms of scale of testing, the median percentage of population tested were 3.28% (women), 1.59% (men) [95% CI: (-1.29%, 3.60%)] with test positive rates of 2.69% (women) and 4.94% (men) respectively. It appears that though statistically not significant, countries led by women have an edge over countries led by men in terms of public health metrics for controlling the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic worldwide.
Keywords: Public health; public policy
overall_justification: This study is clearly about COVID-19 and includes an explicit transmission metric (time-varying effective reproduction number) with quantitative estimates and uncertainty. However, it appears to focus on comparing country leadership groups rather than estimating the basic reproduction number (R0) specifically; it reports effective Rt values.
disease_justification: The title and abstract explicitly focus on the COVID-19 pandemic and control of COVID-19 epidemics across countries.
population_justification: Country-level public health metrics for COVID-19 inherently pertain to human populations, though no specific subgroup is emphasized.
location_justification: The analysis compares women- vs men-led countries worldwide, indicating a multi-country/global setting.
evidence_justification: Uses cross-country data (public health metrics) available up to June 3 and reports bootstrap confidence intervals, suggesting an original empirical analysis rather than a narrative commentary.
transmission_justification: Explicitly reports a time-varying effective reproduction number (median Rt) for women- vs men-led countries, including confidence intervals.

Title: Mathematical modeling of COVID-19 spreading with asymptomatic infected and interacting peoples.
Authors: Serhani M, Labbardi H.
Abstract: In this article we propose a modified compartmental model describing the transmission of COVID-19 in Morocco. It takes account on the asymptomatic people and the strategies involving hospital isolation of the confirmed infected person, quarantine of people contacting them, and home containment of all population to restrict mobility. We establish a relationship between the containment control coefficient c 0 and the basic reproduction number R 0 . Different scenarios are tested with different values of c 0 , for which the stability of a Disease Free Equilibrium point is correlated with the condition linking R 0 and c 0 . A worst scenario in which the containment is not respected in the same way during the period of confinement leads to several rebound in the evolution of the pandemic. It is shown that home containment, if it is strictly respected, played a crucial role in controlling the disease spreading.
Keywords: (SIAQRD) model; COVID-19 virus pandemic; Disease free equilibrium stability; Mathematical modeling of infection disease
overall_justification: The paper is clearly about COVID-19 transmission in a specific human population (Morocco) and explicitly centers R0. However, based on the abstract it is unclear whether R0 is empirically estimated from real-world data versus derived in a theoretical way within a compartmental model, so it is not a high-confidence strong candidate.
disease_justification: Focuses explicitly on COVID-19 transmission (“COVID-19 spreading”, “COVID-19 in Morocco”).
population_justification: Model describes transmission with interventions affecting the “all population” in Morocco (home containment, quarantine, isolation), implying a human population context.
location_justification: Study setting is explicitly Morocco.

transmission_justification: Explicitly discusses the basic reproduction number R0 and derives/uses a relationship between containment control coefficient c0 and R0, including conditions for disease-free equilibrium stability.

Title: Bayesian modeling of COVID-19 cases with a correction to account for under-reported cases.
Authors: de Oliveira ACS, Morita LHM, da Silva EB, Zardo LAR, Fontes CJF, Granzotto DCT.
Abstract: The novel of COVID-19 disease started in late 2019 making the worldwide governments came across a high number of critical and death cases, beyond constant fear of the collapse in their health systems. Since the beginning of the pandemic, researchers and authorities are mainly concerned with carrying out quantitative studies (modeling and predictions) overcoming the scarcity of tests that lead us to under-reporting cases. To address these issues, we introduce a Bayesian approach to the SIR model with correction for under-reporting in the analysis of COVID-19 cases in Brazil. The proposed model was enforced to obtain estimates of important quantities such as the reproductive rate and the average infection period, along with the more likely date when the pandemic peak may occur. Several under-reporting scenarios were considered in the simulation study, showing how impacting is the lack of information in the modeling.
Keywords: Bayesian aproach; COVID-19; SIR model; Under-reporting
overall_justification: The study explicitly analyzes COVID-19 case data in Brazil using a Bayesian SIR framework and states it estimates the reproductive rate (likely R0/related metric). It appears to provide original, data-calibrated estimates rather than commentary or purely theoretical simulation, making it a plausible source for reproduction number information.
disease_justification: Explicitly focuses on COVID-19 (novel coronavirus disease) and modeling of COVID-19 cases.
population_justification: Focuses on COVID-19 cases in Brazil, implying human population surveillance data rather than animal/in vitro work.
location_justification: Study setting is explicitly Brazil (real-world geographic context).
evidence_justification: Uses Brazilian COVID-19 case data and fits a Bayesian SIR model with an under-reporting correction to estimate parameters (i.e., an original empirical modeling analysis, not a review).
transmission_justification: Explicitly states the model was used to estimate "important quantities such as the reproductive rate" (directly aligned with reproduction/reproductive number outcomes).

Title: A Brief Theory of Epidemic Kinetics.
Authors: Louchet F.
Abstract: In the context of the COVID-19 epidemic, and on the basis of the Theory of Dynamical Systems, we propose a simple theoretical approach for the expansion of contagious diseases, with a particular focus on viral respiratory tracts. The infection develops through contacts between contagious and exposed people, with a rate proportional to the number of contagious and of non-immune individuals, to contact duration and turnover, inversely proportional to the efficiency of protection measures, and balanced by the average individual recovery response. The obvious initial exponential increase is readily hindered by the growing recovery rate, and also by the size reduction of the exposed population. The system converges towards a stable attractor whose value is expressed in terms of the "reproductive rate" R0, depending on contamination and recovery factors. Various properties of the attractor are examined, and particularly its relations with R0. Decreasing this ratio below a critical value leads to a tipping threshold beyond which the epidemic is over. By contrast, significant values of the above ratio may bring the system through a bifurcating hierarchy of stable cycles up to a chaotic behaviour.
Keywords: COVID-19; attractor; chaos; contamination kinetics; critical state; dynamical systems; epidemic; herd immunity; reproductive rate; stable cycle
overall_justification: COVID-19 and R0 are explicitly central, but the paper appears to present a theoretical framework rather than an empirical estimate of COVID-19 R0. No geographic context is provided, and there is no clear original data or real-world calibration described, making it unlikely to meet the review’s requirement for original empirical evidence estimating R0.
disease_justification: Explicitly framed around the COVID-19 epidemic (keywords and abstract).
population_justification: Discusses transmission via contacts between contagious and exposed people in the context of an epidemic; implies human population dynamics but does not explicitly specify humans or a study population.
location_justification: No geographic setting or data source is described; appears location-agnostic theory.
evidence_justification: Appears to be a purely theoretical dynamical-systems treatment without empirical estimation/calibration using real-world COVID-19 data described in the abstract.
transmission_justification: Explicitly centers on the “reproductive rate” R0, including expressing an attractor value in terms of R0 and discussing thresholds related to R0.

Title: Estimating the impact of mobility patterns on COVID-19 infection rates in 11 European countries.
Authors: Bryant P, Elofsson A.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: As governments across Europe have issued non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) such as social distancing and school closing, the mobility patterns in these countries have changed. Most states have implemented similar NPIs at similar time points. However, it is likely different countries and populations respond differently to the NPIs and that these differences cause mobility patterns and thereby the epidemic development to change. METHODS: We build a Bayesian model that estimates the number of deaths on a given day dependent on changes in the basic reproductive number, R 0, due to differences in mobility patterns. We utilise mobility data from Google mobility reports using five different categories: retail and recreation, grocery and pharmacy, transit stations, workplace and residential. The importance of each mobility category for predicting changes in R 0 is estimated through the model. FINDINGS: The changes in mobility have a considerable overlap with the introduction of governmental NPIs, highlighting the importance of government action for population behavioural change. The shift in mobility in all categories shows high correlations with the death rates 1 month later. Reduction of movement within the grocery and pharmacy sector is estimated to account for most of the decrease in R 0. INTERPRETATION: Our model predicts 3-week epidemic forecasts, using real-time observations of changes in mobility patterns, which can provide governments with direct feedback on the effects of their NPIs. The model predicts the changes in a majority of the countries accurately but overestimates the impact of NPIs in Sweden and Denmark and underestimates them in France and Belgium. We also note that the exponential nature of all epidemiological models based on the basic reproductive number, R 0 cause small errors to have extensive effects on the predicted outcome.
Keywords: Bayesian model; COVID-19; Infection rate; MCMC simulations; Mobility patterns; Non-pharmaceutical interventions
overall_justification: Meets all core criteria: explicit COVID-19 focus, human population context, clear multi-country setting, empirical data inputs (deaths and mobility), and R0 is central to the model and findings. The study directly estimates/infers R0 changes, aligning closely with an R0-focused review.
disease_justification: Focuses explicitly on COVID-19 infection rates and deaths across multiple European countries.
population_justification: Analyzes population-level COVID-19 outcomes (deaths/infection dynamics) in national populations; no indication of animal/in vitro work.
location_justification: Conducted across 11 European countries (multi-country real-world setting), with country-specific comparisons (e.g., Sweden, Denmark, France, Belgium).
evidence_justification: Uses original modeling analysis combining observed deaths and Google mobility data in a Bayesian framework to estimate R0 changes; appears to be an empirical, data-calibrated study (not a review/commentary).
transmission_justification: The abstract explicitly models and estimates changes in the basic reproductive number (R0) as a function of mobility patterns, repeatedly referencing R0 as a key parameter/output.

Title: Epidemiologic, Clinical, and Laboratory Findings of the COVID-19 in the current pandemic: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
Authors: Xie Y, Wang Z, Liao H, Marley G, Wu D, Tang W.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic has affected the world deeply, with more than 3,000,000 people infected and nearly 200,000 deaths. This review aimed to summarize the epidemiologic traits, clinical spectrum, CT results and laboratory findings of the COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: We scoped for relevant literatures published during 1 st Dec 2019 to 23 rd Apr 2020 based on four databases using English and Chinese languages. We reviewed and analyzed the relevant clinic outcomes of COVID-19. RESULTS: The COVID-19 pandemic was found to have a higher transmission rate compared to SARS and MERS and involved 4 stages of evolution. The basic reproduction number (R 0 ) is 3.32 (95% CI:3.24-3.39), the incubation period was 5.24 days (95% CI:3.97-6.50, 5 studies) on average, and the average time for symptoms onset varied by countries. Common clinical spectrums identified included fever (38.1-39.0°C), cough and fatigue, with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) being the most common complication reported. Body temperatures above 39.0 °C, dyspnea, and anorexia were more common symptoms in severe patients. Aged over 60 years old, having co-morbidities, and developing complications were the commonest high-risk factors associated with severe conditions. Leucopenia and lymphopenia were the most common signs of infection while liver and kidney damage were rare but may cause bad outcomes for patients. The bilateral, multifocal Ground-Glass Opacification (GGO) on peripheral, and the consolidative pulmonary opacity were the most frequent CT results and the tendency of mortality rates differed by region. CONCLUSIONS: We provided a bird's-eye view of the COVID-19 during the current pandemic, which will help better understanding the key traits of the disease. The findings could be used for disease's future research, control and prevention.
Keywords: COVID-19; Clinical spectrum; Epidemiology; Laboratory findings; Nature history
overall_justification: The paper explicitly concerns COVID-19 and reports an R0 estimate (3.32 with 95% CI), making it transmission-metric relevant. However, it is a systematic review/meta-analysis and therefore not original empirical evidence per the review’s inclusion rules, so it is not a strong candidate for extracting primary R0 estimates.
disease_justification: Explicitly investigates COVID-19 throughout (title/abstract), including epidemiologic and clinical findings in the pandemic.
population_justification: Focuses on human COVID-19 cases and summarizes clinical/epidemiologic characteristics (symptoms, complications, risk factors).
location_justification: Systematic review/meta-analysis drawing from multiple databases and likely multiple countries/regions; no geographic restriction stated, but covers global pandemic evidence.
evidence_justification: Explicitly a “Systematic Review and Meta-analysis,” synthesizing existing studies rather than reporting new primary empirical data.
transmission_justification: Directly reports the basic reproduction number (R0) with a pooled estimate and confidence interval.

Title: Dynamics of a fractional order mathematical model for COVID-19 epidemic.
Authors: Zhang Z, Zeb A, Egbelowo OF, Erturk VS.
Abstract: In this work, we formulate and analyze a new mathematical model for COVID-19 epidemic with isolated class in fractional order. This model is described by a system of fractional-order differential equations model and includes five classes, namely, S (susceptible class), E (exposed class), I (infected class), Q (isolated class), and R (recovered class). Dynamics and numerical approximations for the proposed fractional-order model are studied. Firstly, positivity and boundedness of the model are established. Secondly, the basic reproduction number of the model is calculated by using the next generation matrix approach. Then, asymptotic stability of the model is investigated. Lastly, we apply the adaptive predictor-corrector algorithm and fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method to simulate the proposed model. Consequently, a set of numerical simulations are performed to support the validity of the theoretical results. The numerical simulations indicate that there is a good agreement between theoretical results and numerical ones.
Keywords: Adaptive predictor–corrector algorithm; COVID-19 epidemic; Fractional differential equations; Numerical simulations; Stability analysis
overall_justification: The study is clearly about COVID-19 and centrally computes a basic reproduction number (R0). However, based on the abstract it is mainly a theoretical modeling and simulation paper without explicit empirical data or calibration, which does not meet the original-empirical-evidence criterion for estimating R0 from observed data.
disease_justification: The title and abstract explicitly focus on “COVID-19 epidemic” and formulate a COVID-19 transmission model.
population_justification: The abstract discusses a compartmental epidemic model (S/E/I/Q/R) for COVID-19, which typically represents human populations, but it does not explicitly state “humans” or a specific human subgroup.
location_justification: No geographic setting is provided; the model appears generic/not tied to a specific location, so location cannot be confirmed from the abstract.
evidence_justification: Appears primarily theoretical (fractional-order differential equation model, stability analysis, numerical simulations) with no clear indication of calibration to real-world COVID-19 data in the abstract.
transmission_justification: Explicitly states that the “basic reproduction number” is calculated using the next generation matrix approach, which directly targets R0.

Title: [Epidemiological characteristics of COVID-19 in Gansu province].
Authors: Gou FX, Zhang XS, Yao JX, Yu DS, Wei KF, Zhang H, Yang XT, Yang JJ, Liu HX, Cheng Y, Jiang XJ, Zheng YH, Wu B, Liu XF, Li H.
Citation: Zhonghua Liu Xing Bing Xue Za Zhi. 2020 Apr 1;41(0):E032. doi: 10.3760/cma.j.cn112338-20200229-00216. Online ahead of print.
Journal/Book: Zhonghua liu xing bing xue za zhi = Zhonghua liuxingbingxue zazhi
Abstract: Objective: To understand the epidemiological characteristics of COVID-19 cases in different epidemic stages in Gansu province. Methods: Epidemiological investigation was conducted to collect the information of confirmed COVID-19 cases, including demographic, epidemiological and clinical information. Results: As of 25 February 2020, a total of 91 confirmed COVID-19 cases had been reported in Gansu. The epidemic of COVID-19 in Gansu can be divided as three different stages, i.e. imported case stage, imported-case plus indigenous case stage, and indigenous case stage. A total of 63 cases were clustered cases (69.23%), 3 cases were medical staff infected with non-occupational exposure. The initial symptoms included fever (54.95%, 50/91), cough (52.75%, 48/91), or fatigue (28.57%, 26/91), the proportion of each symptom showed a decreasing trend along with the three epidemic stages, but only the differences in proportions of fever (trend χ2=2.20, P<0.05) and fatigue (trend χ2=3.18, P<0.05) among the three epidemic stages were statistically significant. The cases with critical severe symptoms accounted for 42.85% (6/14), 23.73% (14/59) and 16.67% (3/18), respectively, in three epidemic stages, showed a decreasing trend (H=6.45, P<0.05). Also, the incubation period prolonged along with the epidemic stage (F=51.65, P<0.01), but the intervals between disease onset and hospital visit (F=5.32, P<0.01), disease onset and diagnosis (F=5.25, P<0.01) became shorter along with the epidemic stage. Additionally, the basic reproduction number (R0) had decreased from 2.61 in imported case stage to 0.66 in indigenous case stage. Conclusions: The COVID-19 epidemic in Gansu was caused by the imported cases, and about 2/3 cases were clustered ones. No medical worker was observed to be infected by occupational exposure. With the progression of COVID-19 epidemic in Gansu, the change in initial symptom and incubation period suggests, the early screening cannot only depend on body temperature monitoring.
Keywords: COVID-19; Epidemiological characteristic
overall_justification: The paper explicitly studies COVID-19 cases in Gansu and reports quantitative estimates of the basic reproduction number (R0), including values by epidemic stage (e.g., 2.61 to 0.66). It is based on original case investigation data in humans, matching the review’s target outcome (R0).
disease_justification: Focuses explicitly on COVID-19 and confirmed COVID-19 cases in the study setting.
population_justification: Includes confirmed human COVID-19 cases (n=91) with demographic/clinical/epidemiologic information.
location_justification: Study is explicitly set in Gansu province (China) with a defined observation period up to 25 Feb 2020.
evidence_justification: Reports epidemiological investigation data on 91 confirmed cases and presents stage-specific analyses including an estimated R0.
transmission_justification: Explicitly reports the basic reproduction number (R0) and provides numerical estimates by epidemic stage (2.61 down to 0.66).

Title: The impact of long-term non-pharmaceutical interventions on COVID-19 epidemic dynamics and control.
Authors: Childs ML, Kain MP, Kirk D, Harris M, Couper L, Nova N, Delwel I, Ritchie J, Mordecai EA.
Journal/Book: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract: Non-pharmaceutical interventions to combat COVID-19 transmission have worked to slow the spread of the epidemic but can have high socio-economic costs. It is critical we understand the efficacy of non-pharmaceutical interventions to choose a safe exit strategy. Many current models are not suitable for assessing exit strategies because they do not account for epidemic resurgence when social distancing ends prematurely (e.g., statistical curve fits) nor permit scenario exploration in specific locations. We developed an SEIR-type mechanistic epidemiological model of COVID-19 dynamics to explore temporally variable non-pharmaceutical interventions. We provide an interactive tool and code to estimate the transmission parameter, β, and the effective reproduction number, R eff . We fit the model to Santa Clara County, California, where an early epidemic start date and early shelter-in-place orders could provide a model for other regions. As of April 22, 2020, we estimate an R eff of 0.982 (95% CI: 0.849 - 1.107) in Santa Clara County. After June 1 (the end-date for Santa Clara County shelter-in-place as of April 27), we estimate a shift to partial social distancing, combined with rigorous testing and isolation of symptomatic individuals, is a viable alternative to indefinitely maintaining shelter-in-place. We also estimate that if Santa Clara County had waited one week longer before issuing shelter-in-place orders, 95 additional people would have died by April 22 (95% CI: 7 - 283). Given early life-saving shelter-in-place orders in Santa Clara County, longer-term moderate social distancing and testing and isolation of symptomatic individuals have the potential to contain the size and toll of the COVID-19 pandemic in Santa Clara County, and may be effective in other locations.
overall_justification: This paper explicitly models COVID-19 transmission in a specific human population and estimates the effective reproduction number (R_eff) from fitted data. However, it reports R_eff (time-varying/effective) rather than explicitly estimating the basic reproduction number R0, so it may not directly answer an R0-focused review without broader inclusion of Re/Rt estimates.
disease_justification: The title/abstract repeatedly and explicitly focus on COVID-19 transmission and epidemic dynamics.
population_justification: Focuses on community transmission and outcomes (deaths) in a county-level human population context.
location_justification: Study is explicitly set in Santa Clara County, California, and discusses local shelter-in-place timing and exit strategies.
evidence_justification: Uses an SEIR-type mechanistic model fit to Santa Clara County data and reports estimated parameters with CIs, suggesting an original calibrated analysis rather than a narrative discussion.
transmission_justification: Explicitly estimates the effective reproduction number (R_eff) and transmission parameter β, providing a point estimate and 95% CI.

Title: Investigating time, strength, and duration of measures in controlling the spread of COVID-19 using a networked meta-population model.
Authors: Zhang J, Dong L, Zhang Y, Chen X, Yao G, Han Z.
Abstract: Policy makers around the world are facing unprecedented challenges in making decisions on when and what degrees of measures should be implemented to tackle the COVID-19 pandemic. Here, using a nationwide mobile phone dataset, we developed a networked meta-population model to simulate the impact of intervention in controlling the spread of the virus in China by varying the effectiveness of transmission reduction and the timing of intervention start and relaxation. We estimated basic reproduction number and transition probabilities between health states based on reported cases. Our model demonstrates that both the time of initiating an intervention and its effectiveness had a very large impact on controlling the epidemic, and the current Chinese intense social distancing intervention has reduced the impact substantially but would have been even more effective had it started earlier. The optimal duration of the control measures to avoid resurgence was estimated to be 2 months, although would need to be longer under less effective controls.
Keywords: COVID-19; Intervention; Meta-population epidemic model; Network dynamics
overall_justification: The study explicitly estimates the basic reproduction number for COVID-19 using reported case data and a calibrated networked meta-population model in China. It appears to provide original empirical estimates relevant to R0, though the primary aim is intervention impact simulation rather than R0 estimation alone.
disease_justification: Explicitly investigates COVID-19 and controlling its spread.
population_justification: Focuses on spread of COVID-19 in China using human mobility (mobile phone) and reported human case data.
location_justification: Study context is explicitly China (nationwide mobile phone dataset; interventions in China).

Title: De-Escalation by Reversing the Escalation with a Stronger Synergistic Package of Contact Tracing, Quarantine, Isolation and Personal Protection: Feasibility of Preventing a COVID-19 Rebound in Ontario, Canada, as a Case Study.
Authors: Tang B, Scarabel F, Bragazzi NL, McCarthy Z, Glazer M, Xiao Y, Heffernan JM, Asgary A, Ogden NH, Wu J.
Abstract: Since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, most Canadian provinces have gone through four distinct phases of social distancing and enhanced testing. A transmission dynamics model fitted to the cumulative case time series data permits us to estimate the effectiveness of interventions implemented in terms of the contact rate, probability of transmission per contact, proportion of isolated contacts, and detection rate. This allows us to calculate the control reproduction number during different phases (which gradually decreased to less than one). From this, we derive the necessary conditions in terms of enhanced social distancing, personal protection, contact tracing, quarantine/isolation strength at each escalation phase for the disease control to avoid a rebound. From this, we quantify the conditions needed to prevent epidemic rebound during de-escalation by simply reversing the escalation process.
Keywords: COVID-19; mathematical model; pandemics; physical and social distancing relaxation; reopening
overall_justification: This study is centrally about COVID-19 transmission control and explicitly calculates a reproduction number (control reproduction number) over multiple intervention phases using a model fitted to real case time-series data in Ontario. While it may focus on Rc/“control reproduction number” rather than baseline R0, it still provides explicit reproduction-number estimates relevant to transmission intensity.

population_justification: Analyzes population-level COVID-19 case time series and interventions (contact tracing, quarantine, isolation) in humans.
location_justification: Clearly set in Ontario, Canada (case study).
evidence_justification: Uses a transmission dynamics model fitted to observed cumulative case time-series data to estimate parameters and the control reproduction number across phases (an original empirical modeling analysis).

Title: The dynamics of COVID-19 with quarantined and isolation.
Authors: Khan MA, Atangana A, Alzahrani E, Fatmawati.
Abstract: In the present paper, we formulate a new mathematical model for the dynamics of COVID-19 with quarantine and isolation. Initially, we provide a brief discussion on the model formulation and provide relevant mathematical results. Then, we consider the fractal-fractional derivative in Atangana-Baleanu sense, and we also generalize the model. The generalized model is used to obtain its stability results. We show that the model is locally asymptotically stable if R 0 < 1 . Further, we consider the real cases reported in China since January 11 till April 9, 2020. The reported cases have been used for obtaining the real parameters and the basic reproduction number for the given period, R 0 ≈ 6.6361 . The data of reported cases versus model for classical and fractal-factional order are presented. We show that the fractal-fractional order model provides the best fitting to the reported cases. The fractional mathematical model is solved by a novel numerical technique based on Newton approach, which is useful and reliable. A brief discussion on the graphical results using the novel numerical procedures are shown. Some key parameters that show significance in the disease elimination from the society are explored.
Keywords: COVID-19 model; Estimation of the parameters; Fractal-fractional model; Numerical results; Quarantine and isolation
overall_justification: The study explicitly focuses on COVID-19 transmission dynamics and directly estimates the basic reproduction number (R0 ≈ 6.6361) using reported human case data from China. It is a modeling paper but appears calibrated to real-world data and includes an explicit R0 estimate, making it highly aligned with the review question.

population_justification: Analyzes reported COVID-19 cases from China, implying a human population context (not animal/in vitro), though specific subpopulations are not detailed.
